extracted.intended_audience: authors of systematic reviews (especially Cochrane review authors) who assess risk of bias in randomized trials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2) to assess risk of bias for a specific result from randomized trials, covering selection of results, specifying the effect of interest, domain-level signalling questions, algorithms for judgements, and how to reach overall judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting which results to assess within the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Before starting an assessment, authors must select which specific results from included trials to assess; trials usually contribute multiple results and several risk-of-bias assessments may be needed for each trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not select results based on likely judgements. Focus on main outcomes (e.g. those contributing to Summary of findings). It is usually infeasible to assess every result for every trial; choose results according to review priorities (see Chapter 7, Section 7.3.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying the nature of the effect of interest (assignment vs adherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review authors must specify whether they are interested in the effect of assignment to intervention (intention-to-treat effect) or the effect of adhering to the intervention (per-protocol effect), because assessments—especially for the 'deviations from intended interventions' domain—differ according to this choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the effect of principal interest in the review protocol; most reviews will address assignment. Principles of ITT: analyse participants in groups to which randomized and include all randomized participants. When effect of assignment is the interest, prefer results in this order: full ITT result; mITT excluding those with missing outcome data; as-treated/naïve per-protocol or analyses excluding eligible participants last. For per-protocol effects, modern causal methods may be less biased than naïve per-protocol/as-treated analyses; these methods require strong assumptions and are less commonly used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signalling questions: structure and response options
rubrics_metrics.description: Within each domain the tool comprises a series of signalling questions intended to elicit factual information relevant to risk of bias, with prespecified response options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response options: Yes; Probably yes; Probably no; No; No information. 'Not applicable' is available for some follow-up questions. Signalling questions are phrased so a 'Yes' may indicate low or high risk depending on the question. 'Yes' and 'Probably yes' (and 'No' and 'Probably no') have equivalent implications for risk-of-bias; recommended when calculating agreement to treat them as the same. 'No information' should be used only when insufficient details prevent any of the other responses and it would be unreasonable to infer Probably yes/Probably no. Signalling questions should be answered independently and not influence answers to other questions except by determining which subsequent questions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithms, domain judgements, free-text justifications and direction of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithms map combinations of responses to signalling questions (including 'No information') to a proposed domain-level judgement (Low, Some concerns, High). Authors must support answers and judgements with written justifications and can override algorithmic proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the algorithm's proposed judgement but verify and change if appropriate; interpret 'risk of bias' as 'risk of material bias' and comment only on issues likely to affect reliability of conclusions. Provide reasons in free-text boxes; include brief direct quotations from the study when possible and list all sources of information (published reports, registry entries, author contact). Optionally indicate likely direction of bias for each domain and overall, but do not guess direction if no clear rationale exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall risk-of-bias judgement for a result
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall judgement for a result uses the same three-level scale as domains (Low, Some concerns, High) and is determined by domain-level judgements according to explicit mapping rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low risk of bias: low risk for all domains for this result. Some concerns: at least one domain raises some concerns but no domain is at high risk. High risk of bias: at least one domain is judged high risk, or multiple domains have some concerns in a way that substantially lowers confidence in the result. A domain-level judgement implies the overall result has at least that level of risk; authors may override default overall judgements with justification. Present overall judgements in the review and reflect them in analyses and conclusions; they feed into GRADE assessments (Chapter 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the allocation sequence was random; whether allocation sequence was adequately concealed; and whether baseline differences between groups suggest a problem with randomization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sequence generation methods (simple/unrestricted randomization; blocked/restricted randomization; stratified randomization; minimization) and their implementation. Allocation sequence concealment is distinct from blinding and seeks to prevent knowledge of upcoming assignments prior to enrolment; failures (e.g. predictable blocked randomization, unsealed/envelope problems) can allow selective enrolment and bias. Do not interpret chance imbalances as evidence of bias. If baseline characteristics indicate a problem that is inconsistent with chance, consider raising risk-of-bias concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers biases from deviations from intended interventions (performance biases), including administration of non-protocol interventions, failures to implement protocol interventions, or participant non-adherence; depends on the effect of interest (assignment vs adherence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effect of assignment, only consider deviations that are inconsistent with protocol, arise because of the experimental context, and influence the outcome (e.g. differential seeking of experimental treatment). For effect of adherence, assess implementation fidelity, participant adherence, balance of non-protocol interventions, and whether appropriate statistical methods were used. Blinding (participants/carers/deliverers) can reduce such biases but is not always possible; lack of blinding may lead to deviations that bias results. Appropriate analyses for assignment follow ITT principles; inappropriate analyses include as-treated, naïve per-protocol, and analyses based on post-randomization exclusions. Modern causal methods (e.g. instrumental variables) may be needed for adherence effects but require assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants, whether there is evidence the result was biased by missing data, and whether missingness likely depends on true outcome values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reasons for missing data (loss to follow-up, missed visits, unavailable records, death). Assess any procedures used to impute or account for missing data. Do not conflate exclusions from analysis for other reasons (e.g. per-protocol exclusions) with missing outcome data (these are addressed in deviations domain). An ITT label is insufficient; base judgements on signalling questions. Determine when the amount or nature of missing data is small enough to exclude bias, and whether missingness patterns differ between groups or relate to true outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate, whether measurement could have differed between intervention groups, whether outcome assessors were aware of intervention received, and whether assessment was likely influenced by that knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate types of outcomes: patient-reported outcomes are susceptible to bias from awareness of intervention (may lead to at least 'Some concerns' or 'High' if likely influenced); observer-reported outcomes not involving judgement (e.g. mortality, automated tests) are usually not likely influenced; observer-reported outcomes involving judgement (e.g. image reading, clinical exams) are potentially influenced and need judgement about likely impact. Outcomes reflecting provider decisions (hospitalization, stopping treatment) are usually likely influenced if provider is aware. For composite outcomes, consider the contribution and bias risk of each component. Blinding of outcome assessors is considered here (distinct from blinding for deviations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns bias arising from selecting the reported result from among multiple intervention effect estimates that were calculated (based on direction, magnitude, or significance), including selective choice of outcome measurement, time point, instrument, assessor, subscale, or analytic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the trial was analysed according to a pre-specified plan finalized before unblinded outcome data were available; attempt to retrieve trial protocols and statistical analysis plans and compare methods/planned outcomes with reported results. Consider selective reporting across time points, instruments, assessors, subscales, and analytic choices (change scores vs post-intervention adjusted, different covariate adjustments, dichotomizing continuous outcomes using multiple cut-points). Distinguish this selective reporting of a result from selective non-reporting of outcome domains (the latter is addressed at the review level in Chapter 13). If documents lack sufficient detail (e.g. registry lists 'pain' without scale/time), indicate insufficient information alongside signalling responses and contact authors for clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope constraint: fixed set of domains; do not add domains
rubrics_metrics.description: RoB 2 covers a required, fixed set of bias domains and no additional domains should be added to the tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The domains included are: randomization process; deviations from intended interventions; missing outcome data; measurement of the outcome; selection of the reported result. The option to add new domains has been removed; assess these domains for each result and do not create extra domains.
